ch05.note: 破釜沉舟: Xiang Yu, crossing the river in 207 BC, smashed the cooking pots and scuttled the boats so his men could only go forward. The idiom means committing past any possibility of retreat — here, the fear that a cornered Chiang will simply have Hu Hanmin killed.

ch05.anchor: a man goes out to hunt the tiger and is swallowed by it
ch05.note: 打虎不成，反被老虎吞掉 — the risk in a single image. The tiger figure runs through the chapter: Wang Yaqiao begins by proposing to watch tigers fight from the hillside and ends by hunting one.

李烈钧 (1882-1946), a famous Republican general: he raised the first banner of the Second Revolution against Yuan Shikai in 1913 and was a senior figure of the party's old guard. Tang Shaoyi (唐绍仪, 1862-1938) was the Republic's first premier — and was himself assassinated in 1938, by agents generally attributed to Dai Li's service, an end this book does not mention but which fits its pattern exactly.

ch05.anchor: in this life we cannot be born on the same day, but I pray we may die on the same day
ch05.note: The oath of the Peach Garden from the Romance of the Three Kingdoms, where Liu Bei, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei swear that though not born on the same day they will die on the same day. It is the most famous sworn-brotherhood formula in Chinese, and putting it in Dai Li's mouth to Wang Yaqiao is the book's heaviest irony: the reader knows how this brotherhood ends.

胡宗南 (1896-1962), later one of Chiang Kai-shek's most senior field commanders. Chinese reference accounts make Wang Yaqiao, Dai Li and Hu Zongnan sworn brothers in the Shanghai years — see the note in the prologue — so the book's placing of the introduction here is consistent with the popular tradition, though not independently documented.

The book said cavalry in chapter two and says artillery here, for the same enrollment. Both readings are unambiguous in the scan, so the inconsistency is the author's; the outside accounts I could reach say cavalry. Flagged rather than harmonized.

ch05.anchor: the name, they said, was given him by Chiang Kai-shek himself
ch05.note: The name 戴笠 comes from a line in the ancient Yuefu song of friendship between men of unequal station: "you in your carriage, I in my bamboo hat (笠); when we meet, you will get down and bow." Choosing it announces exactly the loyalty across a gulf of rank that Dai Li's career was built on. Whether Chiang chose it is the popular tradition's claim; the classical source is not in doubt.
酒囊饭袋: a man who is nothing but a container for what he consumes. The insult is old and entirely dismissive, and Wang Yaying is using it on her own husband's possible future.

汪精卫 (1883-1944). The chapter's reference to his own assassination attempt is real and famous: in 1910 he was caught trying to blow up the Qing Prince Regent Zaifeng and wrote from prison the lines about dying young and gladly for the cause that made him a national romantic hero. That the man plotting Chiang's murder here is a former assassin himself is exact; that he would end as head of the Japanese-sponsored government at Nanjing is the irony the book leaves for later chapters.

The book's figure for the Guangzhou faction's assassination fund. Chinese accounts of the 1931 plot do describe the Guangzhou opposition financing Wang Yaqiao, and figures in this range circulate; I could not verify the exact sum. Treat the number as the book's.

ch05.anchor: the Iron and Blood Traitor-Purging Corps
ch05.note: 铁血锄奸团. The name is real and belongs to Wang Yaqiao's later organizing, but its dating here is wrong: the corps is associated with the anti-Japanese period from 1932 onward, and "during the Shanghai fighting" points to the January 28 Incident of 1932 — which had not yet happened in the spring of 1931. So Sun Fengming's introduction carries a forward-dated credential. Contradicted as chronology; the man and the organization are both real.

孙凤鸣 (1905-1935), the assassin of chapter thirteen: in November 1935 he shot Wang Jingwei at a Nationalist plenum in Nanjing, having failed to find Chiang Kai-shek, and died of his wounds. His introduction here, four years early and as a quiet young man in spectacles, is the book laying its longest fuse. That he came from the Northeast and was radicalized by its loss to Japan is standard in the accounts.

华克之 (1902-1998), the organizer this chapter turns on: a Nanjing student leader who became the planner of Wang Yaqiao's assassination operations, and the man behind the 1935 attempt in chapter thirteen. He escaped that one, spent the war years underground, later worked for the Communist side, and — alone among the principals of this book — died in bed at ninety-six. Corroborated.

The name as printed is 陈惘; the glyph is legible but the man is not identifiable in the sources I could reach, and the romanization is mine. The larger claim — that Wang Yaqiao's assassination organization by this period contained Communists alongside Hatchet Gang men and patriotic students — is consistent with what is known of his shifting alliances in the 1930s.

The decoy motorcade is a real security practice of the period and is described in accounts of Chiang's movements. The book uses it to explain, plausibly, why a road ambush in Nanjing was abandoned in favor of the airfield.

庐山, the mountain above Jiujiang in Jiangxi, and from 1930 the summer capital of Nationalist China: Chiang Kai-shek governed from it through the hot months, held the famous Lushan conferences there, and drew the whole apparatus of state up the mountain with him. Guling (牯岭), the hill town at its center, had been developed as a foreign missionary and merchant resort from the 1890s, which is why a chapter about Chinese political murder is full of English villas.

滑竿: a seat slung between two carrying poles, the standard conveyance up Chinese mountains before roads. The whole chapter's geography of assassination depends on it — Chiang and Soong ride in chairs at walking pace along narrow paths, which is precisely what makes them shootable.

美庐, the villa the chapter describes accurately: built in 1922 by a British owner on Guling's Route 13, given to Soong Mei-ling around 1930, renamed by her, and used by the Chiangs as their Lushan residence. The name puns — 美 is the 美 of 美龄, Mei-ling, and also means beautiful. It still stands and is a museum. The book's account of its provenance matches the standard local history closely enough to have been taken from it.

The superstition being Western, not Chinese — the ominous Chinese number is four, as the prologue's first note explains. That Soong Mei-ling, American-educated and Methodist, should renumber a house for a Western superstition is a small precise detail of her cultural position.
The Monkey King's seventy-two shape-changes in Journey to the West. Wang Yaqiao means his wife cannot conjure the guns past a search; she is about to prove she can.

金华火腿: the salt-cured hams of Jinhua in Zhejiang, a delicacy for a thousand years and the standard prestige gift of the region — which is exactly why they pass a checkpoint without a second look. The ham stratagem is not the author's invention: Chinese accounts of the 1931 Lushan plot record the guns going up the mountain hidden inside hams, and record too that a discarded ham casing found by the roadside was what put Chiang's guards on alert. Corroborated, and the hinge of the whole episode.

ch05.anchor: the wife of a Nationalist dignitary
ch05.note: The disguise works on an exact social reading: the checkpoints were searching for men and for the poor, and a woman arriving as an official's wife with a concubine, an aide and porters was the one category that could not be handled roughly. The luggage the sentries do open — letters from Chiang, Feng Yuxiang, Zhang Xueliang and Soong Mei-ling — is a forger's masterstroke of the kind the book does not pause to explain.

达姆枪 / 达姆弹. Dumdum properly names the expanding bullet developed at the Dum Dum arsenal near Calcutta and outlawed for warfare by the Hague Declaration of 1899, not a type of gun; and expanding rounds kill by wound trauma, not by poisoning the body within half an hour as this page claims. The book is repeating a popular Chinese misconception of the period — dumdum bullets were widely believed to be poisoned. I translate the claim as written and flag it here rather than silently correcting the author's pharmacology.
美龄号, Chiang Kai-shek's aircraft, named for his wife. The plane was real and the name is well attested; the ambush laid for it here failed because the Chiangs travelled by warship from Pukou instead.

ch05.anchor: die to accomplish benevolence; give up life to hold to the right
ch05.note: 杀身成仁，舍生取义: the first half from the Analects ("the man of purpose does not seek life at the cost of benevolence; he will give his body to complete it"), the second from Mencius ("I will let go life and take righteousness"). Together they are the classical formula for principled self-sacrifice. Assassins swearing an oath in the words of Confucius and Mencius is the exact register of this movement, which understood itself as moral rather than criminal.

俞济时 (1904-1990), a real figure and correctly placed: a Fenghua man connected to Chiang's family, he commanded Chiang's personal guard and later ran the Attendants' Office. He was among the most trusted men in the Nationalist inner circle, and his professional caution in this chapter — the two-party guard, the concealed detail — is what defeats the plot.

宋美龄 (1898-2003), Chiang's wife from 1927, Wellesley-educated and the regime's most effective voice abroad. Her role in this chapter is the author's most interesting structural choice: it is her insistence on breaking the pattern of the daily walk that sends Chiang onto the southwest slope where the killers are waiting — so the woman guarding him and the woman planning his death (Wang Yaying) reason identically about routine, and the two of them decide the chapter between them.

仙人洞, a Lushan grotto associated with the Daoist immortal Lü Dongbin, and one of the mountain's most famous sights; the four-character inscription the text quotes is on the rock there. Mao Zedong's 1961 poem about the "immortal's cave" made it famous a second time to a later generation of Chinese readers.

ch05.anchor: eight or nine empty Jinhua ham casings
ch05.note: The discovery that breaks the plot, and the detail Chinese accounts of the episode preserve. The assassins' one mistake was disposing of the casings where they could be found. Corroborated.

ch05.anchor: whose single word weighed as nine tripods
ch05.note: The same idiom used of Du Yuesheng in chapter four, here applied to Soong Mei-ling inside her own household — and applied, note, to explain why the head of Chiang Kai-shek's bodyguard would not contradict her even when he had found evidence of an armed conspiracy on the mountain. The book is making a point about who actually decided things at the Meilu.

云湖衫, a Hong Kong-made short-sleeved shirt fashionable with the wealthy of Southeast Asia. The garment is what betrays Chen Cheng: right for a rich holidaymaker, wrong for anyone walking a bamboo grove in the rain, and not what a bodyguard wears. A detail of dress decides the chapter.

The attempt is documented. In June 1931 Wang Yaqiao sent men disguised as tourists to kill Chiang Kai-shek on Lushan; the attempt failed when a member of the team acted prematurely and was shot dead by Chiang's guards; the others escaped to Shanghai. Two differences from the book: accounts give the date as June 14, not the 17th, and describe Chen Cheng as having acted without informing the two companions lying in wait — a rashness the book's own narration actually dramatizes in the same terms. Accounts add what the book omits: Chiang ordered the affair kept out of the press and the body buried quietly. Corroborated; the date is off by three days.

陈成, the university student who died on Lushan. He should not be confused with the far more famous general Chen Cheng (陈诚, 1898-1965), one of Chiang Kai-shek's principal commanders — a different man with a different second character. The two names are distinguishable in Chinese and identical in pinyin, which is precisely the kind of collision that makes a romanized name ledger necessary.
